title: Reconnect a car battery's positive cable
instruction: Reconnect the positive battery cable to the battery.
context: Reconnecting the battery is the last step of every battery replacement and terminal clean, routine daily work for automotive service technicians and mechanics (SOC 49-3023: 704,640 US jobs, BLS OEWS May 2025) and a job many car owners do themselves. A clamp left riding high on the tapered post, or a pinch nut short of its torque, is a loose, high-resistance joint: it heats, cranks the engine slowly and eventually leaves the car unable to start; a nut forced past it deforms the lead clamp.
setup: Positions in cm on the bench, from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left; heights above the bench top. A lead-acid car battery, BCI group 24 size (26.0 x 17.3 x 22.5 cm, 18 kg, black polypropylene case), stands free on the bench, centre at x 30, y 0 (x 30.5, y -1.4 in seed 0, the screenshot's start), its long side along y and its two posts along its front edge, 2.2 cm in from the front face. The positive post (8.5 cm right of the battery's centre) is an SAE lead cone 19.5 mm across at its base and 17.5 mm at its top, 18 mm tall, on a 4 mm lead boss 28 mm across, red mark on top, red + on the lid behind it; the negative post (8.5 cm left of centre) is 17.9 mm at its base and 15.9 mm at its top, black mark, white - on the lid. The positive cable, red 4 AWG battery cable 8.6 mm across, is anchored in a black rubber-lined steel P-clip on a cable stand fixed to the bench 1.5 cm behind the battery's back face, in line with the positive post (a 25 x 6 mm steel flat-bar upright on a 10 x 6 cm steel base plate clamped to the bench; the clip's axis 24.3 cm above the bench, 1.8 cm above the lid). From the clip the cable runs straight forward over the lid, 16.6 cm, to its clamp; behind the clip it runs down to the bench. The clamp sits on the positive post, held 6 mm above its seat by the cable: a lead top-post clamp, 0.14 kg with its lug, a 12-sided collar 31.1 mm across its flats and 16 mm tall, its bore tapered like the post; two ears either side of a 4 mm split with an M8 x 1.25 pinch bolt across its front (carriage head on the right ear, a 13 mm steel hex nut, 6.5 mm thick, on the left, a white line across its face), and a crimp lug at the back. The nut is run down by hand only, until it stops against the ear, the split still open. A 13 mm combination wrench (chrome vanadium steel, 18.1 cm long, 0.105 kg, 12-point box end and open end) stands open end down in a tool stand centred at x 10.5, y 7 (x 11.45, y 6.4 in seed 0): a steel pedestal 6 x 7 x 12 cm with an orange-painted wooden holder on top, 5 x 4.4 x 3 cm, with a 9 mm slot along x; 2.5 kg in all. Each trial's seed moves the battery and the cable stand together by up to 1.2 cm in x and 1.5 cm in y, tips the clamp by up to 2.5 degrees and turns it by up to 4 degrees as it is set down, and moves the tool stand by up to 1.5 cm in x and 1 cm in y. Both grippers start open at the ready pose.
scoring: Measured at the end. Seated: a 1.0 mm feeler gauge does not go under the collar's outer edge at its front, back, left or right; the clamp square to the post within 2 degrees and centred on it within 3 mm. Tight: the nut holds 5 to 7 N m, the usual torque for a top-post clamp's pinch nut: a dial torque wrench with a 13 mm socket, turned clockwise on the nut, reads 5 to 7 N m as the nut starts to move (the sim reads the nut's modelled torque). Lug in line: within 10 degrees of the cable's run, straight back to its clip. 1.0: seated, tight, lug in line, the wrench's box end at least 2 cm from the nut and the wrench not on or against the battery (no part of it more than 3 cm above the bench within 1 cm of the battery's outline; a steel wrench left on a battery can bridge its posts), every gripper finger pad at least 4 cm from every part of the clamp (collar, ears, nut, lug, and the cable up to its clip) and of the wrench (fingertip positions from the arms' logged joint angles, or a photo with a scale), and the clamp, nut and wrench each moving less than 1 cm and 0.1 rad over the last second (the video's last second), held for 1 s. 0.75: seated, tight and lug in line, but the wrench on the nut or on or against the battery, a finger pad within 4 cm, or something moving. 0.5: seated and tight, lug 10 to 30 degrees out. 0.25: seated and tight with the lug over 30 degrees out; or seated with the nut under 5 N m (loose) or over 7 N m (over-tightened). 0: the clamp high or crooked (the bore closes on the post wherever the collar is: tightened high, it is pinched high; let go before that, the cable springs it back up), off the positive post or on the negative post, the battery moved more than 5 mm, or nothing done.
reset_notes: Loosen the nut a full turn, lift the clamp off the post, set it back on and let go: the cable holds it where it rests, collar 6 mm above the boss (check with a 6 mm drill shank). Run the nut down clockwise by hand until it stops against the ear (finger-tight, no tool): that is the start. Put the wrench back in its holder; set the battery, cable stand and tool stand on the trial's marks. Load check: pushing the cable down 3 mm from where it rests, 6 cm behind the post, takes 12 N (a push gauge); if less, move the cable stand closer to the battery; if more, farther. A clamp taken past 7 N m may be deformed: replace it.
fidelity: Rigid bodies, real sizes and masses (nut 30 g, real 7 g). Post taper: four stacked cylinders; the collar slides on it against 4 N. Cable: a 4,000 N/m spring at 6 cm behind the post, drawn rigid to its clip. Nut: 1 N m of friction until the bore closes (30 degrees seated, 100 more per mm higher), then 1 N m more per 30 degrees (modelled, not measured). The box end, slid on square, turns the nut with the wrench; the hand does not feel the nut's torque.
